Updates

What shipped, and why it matters

Short notes on Amazon EVS, VMware Cloud on AWS and VCF releases, each with a link to the source.

November 2026

Nov 24, 2026VCFVMware · AI

VCF 9.1.2 is out#

Broadcom shipped VCF 9.1.2 today. Most of it is aimed at getting AI and Kubernetes platforms up faster:

  • An AI infrastructure quickstart: one vCenter plugin configures the cluster, turns on Supervisor and builds a VKS cluster.
  • A VKS quickstart that gives you a working Supervisor and VKS cluster, plus a test environment with add-ons.
  • Chained VKr upgrades. Pick the version you want and VCF works out the steps to get there.
  • The GitOps service (Argo CD inside VCF) and vSAN's S3-compatible object storage are now GA. Both were tech previews in 9.1.1.

The object storage piece is the one I'd pay attention to even if AI isn't on your roadmap. Backups, logs and cloud-native apps can use S3 buckets on vSAN, so you don't need a separate object store for them.

Source
  • Broadcom blog: Announcing General Availability of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.2
Nov 24, 2026vCloudOneVMware · Cloud

New on vCloudOne: sizing calculators#

I've added three sizers to the site, one each for Amazon EVS, VMware Cloud on AWS and on-prem VCF. Drop in RVTools exports or type in workload totals and you get hosts, clusters and management overhead, with checks and an Excel export.

  • EVS Sizing: hosts and clusters for Amazon EVS.
  • VMC Sizing: SDDCs, clusters and hosts, with placement and DR per workload group, a topology diagram and a memory tiering estimate per cluster.
  • VCF Sizing: fleets, instances, domains and clusters on your own hardware, plus licensing and add-on overhead.

Everything runs in your browser, so customer data stays on your machine. The VMC and VCF sizers explain each default when you hover over it, and the Excel export keeps your settings so you can load the sizing again later. I built them for architects and partners who need a quick first sizing they can defend. Confirm with the official tools before anything goes in a quote.

SDDC 1.26v5 is the new default build#

New SDDCs and upgrades now get SDDC 1.26v5. It's a security patch build with no new features, so mostly a note for whoever tracks SDDC versions across the estate.

Nov 20, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

You can now raise the Elastic DRS storage warning#

The Elastic DRS storage warning on VMware Cloud on AWS used to be fixed at 65%. You can now move it up to 75% through the Autoscaler API.

On storage-heavy SDDCs, that 65% warning can go off during normal operation. Now you can set it closer to the point where you'd actually act. Because it's an API setting, it's easy to roll out across several SDDCs at once.

Source
  • VMware Cloud on AWS release notes: November 20, 2026
Nov 17, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware · AI

Amazon EVS gets r7i hosts, external principal storage and an Agent Skill#

Amazon EVS now supports r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl for VCF 9.x. These are memory-optimized hosts with no local NVMe, so AWS also added support for external principal storage. In practice that means Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP instead of vSAN. The EVS Deployment Orchestrator can create the FSx file system for you, and with FSx a simple deployment needs only 2 hosts.

Until now you bought compute and vSAN storage together. With r7i and FSx you can size them separately, so memory-heavy workloads don't pay for NVMe they won't use, and storage can grow without adding hosts. If you already run FSx for ONTAP, this is the easiest way to get storage off the hosts.

The same launch included an Amazon EVS Agent Skill. You point your AI agent at the skill file in the EVS GitHub repo, and it can answer planning questions, suggest designs, write blueprints and run deployments through the orchestrator. If you're automating EVS builds, it's worth trying.

Sources
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS launches support for r7i.metal instances, external principal storage, and an Agent Skill
  • GitHub: Solutions for Amazon EVS release v1.1.0
Nov 4, 2026VCFVMware

vSphere Express, Live Recovery and DR built into VCF#

Broadcom announced a few changes to the VCF portfolio:

  • vSphere Express, a new entry edition on vSphere 9 for up to 128 cores. It includes vMotion, HA, distributed switching and TPM security.
  • Two new Advanced Services: VMware Live Recovery for disaster and cyber recovery, and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management.
  • Disaster recovery built into VCF and VVF themselves, planned for the next release.

Express gives small sites and branch offices a supported starting point that can move up to VVF or VCF later. The native DR piece is the one I'll be watching, since it could change how people design and license recovery.

Sources
  • Broadcom blog: VCF portfolio update
  • Network World: Broadcom expands VMware Cloud Foundation with AI, security, and recovery capabilities

Amazon EVS adds Osaka, Taipei, Spain and Tel Aviv#

Amazon EVS added four more Regions: Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Taipei), Europe (Spain) and Israel (Tel Aviv).

Add December's seven and July's three, and that's fourteen new Regions in a year. More Regions help with data residency, and with DR designs that need a second Region close by.

Source

Sep 3, 2026VCFVMware · AI

VCF 9.1.1 lands the week of VMware Explore#

VCF 9.1.1 came out the same week as VMware Explore in Las Vegas, and most of what's new is AI:

  • Multi-Tenant Model Sharing lets several business units use one model deployment while keeping their data separate.
  • AI Assistant for VCF is a chat assistant inside VCF Operations, and you choose the model provider.
  • GitOps and native object storage showed up as tech previews. Both went GA in 9.1.2.

For most infrastructure teams, 9.1.1 is simply the maintenance build to land on after 9.1. The AI features need VCF Private AI Services, so they matter most if private AI is already on your plan.

Source
  • Broadcom blog: Announcing General Availability of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1

August 2026

Aug 27, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

i7i.metal-48xl and the EVS Deployment Orchestrator#

Two things landed around Amazon EVS's first birthday. The i7i.metal-48xl is a bigger host on 5th Gen Intel Xeon, so you can run more VMs on fewer hosts. AWS says i7i gives up to 23% better compute and more than 10% better price performance than i4i.

AWS also released the EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO) in the Solutions for Amazon EVS repo. You launch one CloudFormation stack and it builds the AWS networking, the hosts and VCF 9.0 or 9.1. A full build takes about 4 to 7 hours and runs unattended.

The 48xl is double the 24xl, which helps big clusters and memory tiering designs fit inside the 32-host limit. EDO matters because the VCF 9 install is now yours to do. If you want builds you can repeat without babysitting them, this is the way to go.

Sources
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS now supports i7i.metal-48xl
  • AWS blog: A year of expanding choice for VMware customers on AWS
  • AWS blog: One Stack, Full VCF: Deploying VCF 9 on Amazon EVS with the EVS Deployment Orchestrator
Aug 21, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Three good reads: NSX Federation, DR and memory tiering on EVS#

AWS put out three design posts for Amazon EVS in one week:

  • Aug 18: NSX Federation on EVS. One Global Manager spans on-prem and EVS sites, with shared segments and firewall policy.
  • Aug 19: A walk-through of DR options for VMware workloads on EVS, from nothing pre-deployed to a full standby cluster.
  • Aug 21: Using VCF 9 memory tiering to fit more VMs on each host.

These answer the questions that usually come up once the migration is done: how to stretch networks and security across sites, how much standby capacity DR really needs, and how far tiering can push density. One thing to remember on EVS is that NVMe you give to memory tiering comes out of vSAN, so size tiering and storage together.

Sources
  • AWS blog: Amazon EVS with NSX Federation for Disaster Recovery and Multi-site Networking
  • AWS blog: Disaster Recovery for VMware Workloads on Amazon EVS
  • AWS blog: Increase your cluster density with Memory Tiering in Amazon EVS

Jul 6, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Amazon EVS now runs VCF 9.0 and 9.1#

This is the big one for Amazon EVS this year. You can now run VCF 9.0 and 9.1 in every Region where EVS is available. EVS sets up the hosts and VPC networking, and you install VCF with Broadcom's VCF Installer. VCF evaluation mode is supported too, which is handy for proofs of concept.

VCF 9 brings memory tiering and the rest of the 9.x platform to AWS, and that's what a lot of customers have been waiting for. The catch is that the VCF install is now your job, so have the installer steps and your VCF subscription sorted before the hosts are ready.

Sources
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS VCF 9.0 and 9.1 support
  • AWS blog: Announcing support for VCF 9.0 and 9.1 on Amazon EVS

May 26, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

You can now take EVS VCF issues straight to Broadcom#

Until now every Amazon EVS case went through AWS Support. If you have an active VCF subscription, you can now open VCF software cases directly with Broadcom. AWS Support still covers the whole stack, and Broadcom covers only the VCF software.

For a pure VCF software problem, going straight to Broadcom can save a hop. Anything about EC2 hosts, VPC networking or the EVS API still goes to AWS, so it helps to agree internally on who opens which kind of case.

Source
  • AWS blog: Amazon EVS expands support options with Broadcom
May 18, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Amazon EVS environments can now grow to 32 hosts#

The host limit per Amazon EVS environment went from 16 to 32, through a service quota increase. You can run one big cluster or split the hosts across several.

Fewer, bigger environments mean fewer sets of management appliances to run and patch. If you've outgrown 16 hosts, or you're running several small environments that could be one, ask for the quota before you need it.

Source
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS enables support for 32 hosts per environment
May 5, 2026VCFVMware · AI

VCF 9.1 is here#

Broadcom announced VCF 9.1, the first feature release since 9.0. It went GA later in May with an in-place upgrade from 9.0. The parts I'd look at first:

  • Better memory tiering. You can turn it on without a reboot, and you can mirror the tier device in software.
  • vSAN deduplication and compression on more cluster types.
  • Live patching for ESX on TPM-enabled hosts, continuous compliance, and ransomware recovery on-prem.
  • Bigger fleet and upgrade limits per VCF instance, faster VM and Kubernetes deployment, and S3 object storage as a tech preview.

9.1 is where memory tiering becomes practical for production. There's no reboot to enable it, and mirroring protects you if a tier drive fails without needing a RAID controller. It's also one of the two versions Amazon EVS added in July, so if you're on VCF at all, this is the release to plan around.

Sources
  • Broadcom blog: VCF 9.1: The Secure, Cost-Effective Private Cloud Platform for Production AI
  • VCF 9.1 release notes: What's New

April 2026

Apr 27, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Amazon EVS adds the i7i.metal-24xl#

Amazon EVS now supports i7i.metal-24xl, a smaller host than i4i on a newer CPU, aimed at better cost-performance for VMware workloads.

The size matters as much as the speed. VCF is subscribed per core, so fewer, faster cores per host can lower your licensing bill as well as your host count. If per-core cost is a big part of your business case, run the numbers on this one.

Source
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS now supports i7i.metal-24xl
Apr 20, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Windows Server licenses on Amazon EVS#

You can now get Windows Server licenses from AWS for VMs running on Amazon EVS, whether you migrate them in or build them new. You add an entitlement per VM through an EVS vCenter connector, and billing is per vCPU-hour while the VM runs.

This solves a real gap. VMs without license portability rights used to need a separate licensing plan, and now you can cover them inside EVS and drop the entitlement when you don't need it. VMs where you bring your own license don't cost anything extra from AWS.

Sources
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS now offers Microsoft Windows Server Licensing
  • AWS blog: Windows Server licensing step-by-step guide
Apr 16, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

Usage Report APIs for VMware Cloud on AWS#

VMware Cloud on AWS has two new usage APIs: a Miscellaneous Usage Report for extra charges like Elastic IPs, Transit Gateway and data transfer, and a Microsoft SPLA Usage Report. They sit alongside the Host Usage Report API from last November.

You get daily usage data you can filter, so VMC spend can go into the same cost and BI tools as the rest of your cloud bill instead of waiting on invoices. If you're the one answering "why did the bill go up," this is for you.

HCX 4.11.4 for VMware Cloud on AWS#

HCX 4.11.4 is a maintenance release. Like 4.11.3 before it, there's no WAN optimization appliance, so if any of your service meshes still have WAN-OPT, remove it before you upgrade. Worth checking if you're in the middle of a migration to VMC.

Source

Apr 1, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

i7i.metal-24xl comes to VMware Cloud on AWS#

With SDDC 1.26v2, VMware Cloud on AWS supports i7i.metal-24xl for new and existing SDDCs in select Regions. It comes with host-to-host encryption, vSAN data-at-rest encryption and Intel TME memory encryption.

A few things to know before you plan on it. Existing SDDCs need to be on 1.26v2 first. vSAN ESA is only for new SDDCs or new secondary clusters. Hyper-threading is on by default, giving 96 logical cores per host. And stretched clusters on i7i use vSAN OSA.

If you're on i3, i3en or i4i and thinking about a host refresh, this is the newer host to look at. It's also a good option for new SDDCs.

Sources
  • Broadcom blog: Announcing the i7i.metal-24xl Instance for VMware Cloud on AWS
  • VMware Cloud on AWS release notes: April 1, 2026

March 2026

Mar 25, 2026vCloudOneHyperscalers · VMware

Amazon EVS deployment prerequisites guide#

I wrote up everything Amazon EVS checks before it deploys VCF 5.x, in the order you'll need it: account and support plan, IAM, IP planning, VPC and subnets, Route 53, DHCP, VPC Route Server and BGP, capacity reservations, licensing and key pairs. It comes with a Terraform kit and a prerequisite validator.

EVS validates all of this up front and fails fast if something is missing, so getting the prep right the first time saves a lot of back and forth. If you're deploying VCF 9, use the VCF Installer or the EVS Deployment Orchestrator instead, since the guide covers the VCF 5.x flow.

January 2026

Jan 23, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Multiple NSX Tier-0 gateways on Amazon EVS#

You can now run more than one NSX Tier-0 gateway in an EVS environment, each on its own Edge cluster.

That gives you two things. You can spread north-south traffic across gateways for more throughput, and you can keep production and non-production, or different tenants, on separate routing and security policies. If you've been running separate environments just to keep routing apart, this may let you consolidate.

Source
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS now supports multiple VMware NSX Edge Gateways
Jan 20, 2026VCFVMware

VCF 9.0.2 maintenance release#

VCF 9.0.2 is a fix release, but two changes in vCenter 9.0.2 are worth knowing about. Certificates issued by the VMware Certificate Authority for vCenter and ESX now renew on their own before they expire, and Supervisor control plane backup is on by default.

Expired certificates cause more outages than they should, so automatic renewal is a welcome change. If you're still on 9.0.0 or 9.0.1, this is the build to plan for.

Source
  • vCenter 9.0.2 release notes
Jan 20, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Pick your VCF and ESX versions on Amazon EVS#

When you create an EVS environment or add hosts, you can now pick a supported VCF and ESX version combination, from the console or the CreateEnvironment API.

This helps most during a migration, when you want EVS on the same version you run on-prem. It also means hosts you add later can stay on the same build as the ones you already have, instead of whatever is newest.

Source
  • AWS What's New: Amazon EVS now supports VCF and VMware ESX software version selection
Jan 16, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

SDDC 1.26: vSAN ESA, bring your own key and VM hardware 21#

SDDC 1.26 moves VMware Cloud on AWS to vSphere 8.0 Update 3, and it brings a lot with it:

  • vSAN ESA is GA, with RAID-5 from 3 hosts. It's the default for new i4i deployments, for non-stretched SDDCs only.
  • Bring your own key: VM encryption with an external KMIP key management system.
  • VM hardware version 21, with up to 256 disks per VM and NVMe for Windows Server Failover Clustering.
  • VMware Tools 12.5.4.

ESA is the change that affects sizing. Every drive is capacity and RAID-5 starts at three hosts, so small clusters get noticeably more usable storage than they did on OSA. Stretched SDDCs stay on OSA, so keep that in mind if you're comparing designs. BYOK is the other one to note if your security team insists on holding its own keys.

Sources
  • Broadcom blog: VMware Cloud on AWS: SDDC Version 1.26 Release
  • VMware Cloud on AWS release notes: January 16, 2026

Dec 2, 2025VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

VMware Cloud on AWS: December 2025 roundup#

Broadcom's December roundup for VMware Cloud on AWS had a few useful changes:

  • A redesigned console at vmc.broadcom.com.
  • Stretched clusters can now scale down to 4 hosts (2 per AZ) or 2 hosts (1 per AZ), with some limits.
  • HCX 4.11.3 drops WAN optimization and is supported until October 11, 2027.
  • Better estimates for moving from i3.metal to i3en.metal or i4i.metal.

The smaller stretched clusters are the part I like most. A multi-AZ SDDC is now a lot cheaper to start with. If you use HCX, check your service meshes for WAN-OPT before you upgrade, because it has to come out first. And if you're still on i3.metal, the new estimates make it easier to plan the move off it.

Source
  • Broadcom blog: VMware Cloud on AWS: What's New (December 2025)
